title: Longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging with ultra-large cranial window for head-fixed mice
author: Hattori, Komiyama
materials: Dental acrylic cement (Contemporary Ortho-Jet™ Powder and Liquid)

steps.title: Generate double transgenic mice
steps.instruction: Cross CaMKIIα‑tTA transgenic mice with tetO‑GCaMP6s transgenic mice to obtain double‑transgenic offspring that express GCaMP6s in most cortical excitatory neurons; select genetic background appropriate for the cell type of interest.

steps.title: Fabricate glass plug
steps.instruction: Make a three‑layer glass plug (two protrusion glasses + one base glass) using #2 and #1 coverslips, cut to the desired shape, glue with UV‑curable adhesive, and store in 70 % ethanol until surgery.

substeps.instruction: Draw the desired window shape (e.g., hexagon) on tape with a pen.
Place a #2 coverslip (~220 µm thick) over the drawing, tape it down, and scrape the glass along the outline with a diamond scribe and ruler.
Detach the #2 coverslip, then crack it along the scribed lines with forceps to obtain protrusion glass pieces; make many pieces and keep those that fit the target size.
Repeat the above using a #1 coverslip (~150 µm thick) with a drawing enlarged by ~1 mm to create the base glass.
Clean all glass pieces with a Kimwipe moistened with 70 % ethanol; ensure no dust remains.
Place < 1 µL of UV glue on the centre of the base glass (remove air bubbles by centrifuging the glue at 3 000 × g for 5 s).
Carefully place one protrusion glass onto the glue, avoiding bubbles, and cure with UV light for 5–10 s (adjust time according to glue and lamp intensity).
Repeat the glue‑place‑cure step to add the second protrusion glass, then remove excess glue from the base with fine forceps.
Verify that the stacked plug has a total height of ~440 µm (sufficient to span skull thickness and apply gentle pressure).
Store the completed glass plug in 70 % ethanol until it is needed for surgery.

steps.title: Sterilize tools and prepare sponge
steps.instruction: Sterilize all surgical equipment and ready gelatin sponge pieces for use during the craniotomy.

substeps.instruction: Wipe the surgery table and stereotaxic frame with 70 % ethanol.
Sterilize forceps, scissors, scalpel, double‑ended carver, head bar, and drill bits using a hot‑bead sterilizer.
Cut gelatin sponge into ~1 mm square pieces and soak them in sterile saline.

steps.title: Anesthetize and expose skull
steps.instruction: Prepare the mouse for craniotomy by anesthetizing, administering prophylactics, cleaning the head, and removing overlying skin and muscles to expose a large dorsal skull area.

substeps.instruction: Induce anesthesia in an adult mouse (> 2 months) with 3 % isoflurane in oxygen in an induction chamber.

Transfer the mouse to the stereotaxic apparatus, secure the nose with a clamp, and maintain anesthesia at 1 %–1.5 % isoflurane delivered via the nose clamp; keep body temperature constant with a servo‑controlled heating pad.
Inject Baytril (10 mg kg⁻¹) and dexamethasone (2 mg kg⁻¹) subcutaneously to prevent infection and inflammation.
Disinfect the head skin with 70 % ethanol followed by betadine, and apply Vaseline to the eyes to prevent drying.
Using scissors, cut away and remove the skin over the dorsal skull (olfactory bulb, cortex, cerebellum).
Wipe the exposed skull surface with a Kimwipe soaked in 70 % ethanol.
Detach the muscles on the lateral edges of the cerebellum to increase exposed skull area; leave the detached posterior muscles in place.
Detach the lateral muscles near the auditory cortex; leave them at their original location (Krazy glue and dental cement will later fill the pocket between these muscles and the skull).
Scrape off all connective tissue from the skull surface with a scalpel, ensuring complete removal.
Rinse and clean the skull surface again with a Kimwipe moistened with 70 % ethanol.

description: Two-photon calcium imaging is a powerful approach to measure neuronal activity at high spatial resolution (Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012; Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006). The technique relies on fluorescent calcium indicators that alter their fluorescence in response to changes in the intracellular calcium concentration. Calcium ions flow into the intracellular compartment through voltage-gated channels in response to neuronal spiking activity. The subcellular resolution of two-photon microscopy and the fluorescent calcium indicators allow the indirect measurement of spiking activity. Furthermore, the activity of the same neurons can be tracked reliably for many weeks and months, which is challenging with electrode recordings. In this paper, we describe a protocol for longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging through an ultra large glass window from behaving mice. The large glass window preparation allows optical access to most dorsal cortical areas in individual mice (Hattori and Komiyama, 2022a; Hattori et al., 2019). The protocol was inspired by an earlier study that described a similar approach (Kim et al., 2016). We describe the step-by-step procedures of the surgery and the imaging experiments.
